question.text:
CASE STUDY (continued): Mrs. Lakshmi has no nominee registered in any of her three mutual fund folios. She has two children — a son and a daughter — and wants to split her holdings equally between them in case of her death.
Question 3: What should Mrs. Lakshmi do regarding nomination, and what are the implications if she does not nominate?

answer.text: Nomination is optional for senior citizens, so she can ignore it without any consequences
She can nominate only one person per folio, so she must choose either her son or daughter

She should nominate both children with 50% allocation each in all folios; without nomination, units are transmitted to the legal successors only after completion of the required transmission documentation
She should create a joint holding with her children instead of nomination

explanation.text: The Logic: An investor may appoint multiple nominees in a folio with a specified percentage distribution, and the nomination applies to all investments in that folio. Mrs. Lakshmi can therefore nominate her son and daughter with 50% each across all three folios. If no nomination is in place, the units are transmitted to the legal successors only after the AMC/RTA receives the required transmission documentation. The Trap: Nomination does not override a will. The nominee receives the units in trust for the legal heirs; the eventual distribution among heirs is governed by succession law or by a valid will, not by the nomination itself. Note: Nomination is a non-financial transaction processed by the AMC/RTA, and it greatly simplifies the transmission process for the surviving family.
